note: Delia Spencer married Arthur Caton in 1876; Arthur, lawyer, sportsman and clubman, loved golf and bred horses and dogs. Meeker: at a Caton dinner Field was reluctant to make a speech, and Delia 'sprang to her feet and said: 'Mr. Field just wants me to remind you that the White Sale starts next Monday''; the Catons had no children and entertained in 'their big, elaborate house on Calumet Avenue'; Meeker's mother 'always declared that nobody ever gave such wonderful parties as Delia Caton'; 'he fell in love with his friend's wife years before he was able to marry her'; 'it was even absurdly asserted that an underground tunnel connected the Caton house on Calumet with the Field house on Prairie, which was just in front of it, or just back'; 'In the Nineties, divorce was unthinkable: they had to wait for him (Arthur Caton) to die, which, distressingly, he didn't do until 1904'. Rumours of suicide abounded. The marriage licence acquired in London in 1905 gave Delia as 46 and Field as 70; they married at St. Margaret's, Westminster, quietly, with a few friends. Field died in 1906 of pneumonia after a golf foursome that included Robert Todd Lincoln; Delia received $1 million and the Field mansion on Prairie Avenue; she left Chicago for Washington, D.C. (the 'Pink Palace'), and died in 1937. A Healy portrait shows her before 1894.
